title: Syncope: red flags, the first tests, and who goes home

source.citation: Written for Blackout, 2026-09-13. Based on the 2017 ACC/AHA/HRS syncope guideline. Not tied to an article; review before trusting.

questions.q: Which are part of the initial evaluation of every patient with syncope?
a: Physical examination with orthostatic vital signs
questions.why: These three identify the cause in about half of patients and are the only tests recommended for all. Everything else is ordered for a reason found in them.

questions.q: Which features point to a cardiac cause of syncope?
a: A family history of sudden death before 50
d: A prodrome of nausea and sweating
Onset after standing a long time in heat
questions.why: Palpitations before the event, known structural heart disease and an abnormal ECG complete the list. The distractors are the classic vasovagal story.

questions.q: What is the most common cause of syncope in a young, otherwise healthy patient?
questions.why: Education and counterpressure manoeuvres, such as leg crossing and hand gripping at the first warning, are the treatment. Drugs add little.

questions.q: Orthostatic hypotension is a fall in systolic pressure of at least how much within three minutes of standing?
questions.why: Or a fall in diastolic of 10 mm Hg. Dehydration and drugs are the usual causes; alpha blockers, diuretics, nitrates and tricyclics are the first to review.

questions.q: When is an echocardiogram indicated after syncope?
questions.a: When structural heart disease is suspected from the history, examination or ECG
questions.why: A murmur, heart failure, an abnormal ECG or exertional syncope are the triggers. Routine echocardiography in an otherwise normal work-up has a very low yield.

questions.q: A patient faints, recovers within a minute, and has a normal neurological examination. Is a head CT indicated?
questions.a: No; neuroimaging is not part of the routine work-up of syncope
questions.why: Syncope comes from global hypoperfusion; strokes and tumours rarely cause it. Imaging is for focal signs or head injury from the fall.

questions.q: Which feature distinguishes a seizure from syncope most reliably?
questions.a: A prolonged period of confusion after the event
questions.why: Brief myoclonic jerks are common in syncope and fool witnesses. Lateral tongue biting and a long post-event confusion favour seizure.

questions.q: Recurrent unexplained syncope with a normal initial work-up and a low suspicion of arrhythmia. Which test helps confirm reflex syncope?
questions.why: For recurrent unexplained syncope where arrhythmia is possible, an implantable loop recorder catches the rhythm at the time of the event and beats short-term monitoring.

questions.q: Which ECG findings in a patient with syncope warrant specialist referral?
d: Sinus bradycardia at 55 in an athlete
questions.why: Each marks a substrate for a dangerous arrhythmia. A normal ECG is reassuring but does not exclude an intermittent arrhythmia.

questions.q: A 70-year-old faints when turning his head or shaving. Which bedside test is appropriate?
questions.a: Carotid sinus massage with ECG and blood pressure monitoring
questions.why: Carotid sinus hypersensitivity is common over 40. A pause over three seconds or a large pressure fall reproduces the symptoms; a pacemaker helps the cardioinhibitory form.

questions.q: Syncope while coughing, urinating or swallowing. What is this?
questions.why: It behaves like vasovagal syncope with a specific trigger. Avoiding the trigger where possible, sitting to urinate at night, and treating the cough are the management.

questions.q: Which patient with syncope should be admitted?
questions.a: One with a suspected cardiac cause
d: Anyone who was injured in the fall
questions.why: Known structural heart disease, an abnormal ECG, exertional syncope or an unexplained event with red flags each justify monitored observation. Clear vasovagal syncope goes home.
